classification.short: Predicting a category (readmitted or not) rather than a number. Many classifiers first estimate a probability, then a threshold turns it into a class.
classification.more: Lecture §1. Two classes is binary classification, the focus of this activity.

positive-class.short: The outcome of interest: the event we want the model to find, such as “readmitted within 30 days”.
positive-class.more: “Positive” does not mean good. Like a positive test result, it means the thing we were looking for was found. Name the positive class first: every metric except accuracy changes meaning if you flip it. Lecture §3.

prevalence.short: The share of patients in the positive class. For example, 9% of discharges were readmitted within 30 days.
prevalence.more: Precision depends on prevalence: the same model gives fewer real flags out of every 100 when the outcome is rarer. Lecture §4.

probability.short: The classifier's estimate of a patient's chance of the positive class, between 0 and 1.
probability.more: It is an estimate. Whether a predicted 30% really means about 30 in 100 such patients needs its own check: a calibration plot. Lecture §1 and §10.

threshold.short: The cut-off that turns a probability into a class: predict positive (“flag”) when the probability is at or above it.
threshold.more: 0.50 is a choice people make, not something the model learns. Moving the threshold changes no probability and needs no retraining. Lecture §1 and §6.

accuracy.short: The fraction of predictions that were correct: (TP + TN) ÷ all patients.
accuracy.more: Accuracy can be useful when the classes are roughly balanced and both kinds of mistake matter about equally. It cannot tell you which mistakes the model makes. Lecture §2.

accuracy-trap.short: With imbalanced classes, a model that finds no one can still score high accuracy. If 91% were not readmitted, saying “no” to everyone is 91% accurate.
accuracy-trap.more: Lecture §2. Always compare an accuracy with the “most common class for everyone” baseline.

majority-baseline.short: The simplest rule there is: predict the most common class for every patient, such as “not readmitted”. Its accuracy is the share of that class.
majority-baseline.more: Before trusting any accuracy number, compute what this rule scores. Lecture §2.

class-imbalance.short: One class is much more common than the other, such as 9 readmitted for every 91 not.

confusion-matrix.short: A 2 × 2 table comparing what the model said with what happened. In this course, rows are the actual class and columns the predicted class.
confusion-matrix.more: Every patient lands in one of four groups: TP, FN, FP or TN. Correct results sit on the diagonal. scikit-learn's confusion_matrix(y, pred) uses another order ([[TN, FP], [FN, TP]]), so always read the labels before the numbers. Lecture §3.

tp.short: The model flagged the patient, and the patient had the outcome. A case caught.

fn.short: The model did not flag the patient, but the patient had the outcome. A missed case.

fp.short: The model flagged the patient, but the patient did not have the outcome. A false alarm.

tn.short: The model did not flag the patient, and the patient did not have the outcome. Correctly left alone.

sensitivity.short: Of the patients who actually had the outcome, the share the model flagged: TP ÷ (TP + FN).
sensitivity.more: Three names, one metric: sensitivity, recall and true positive rate (TPR). Its denominator is the top row of the matrix. Lecture §4.

specificity.short: Of the patients who did not have the outcome, the share the model correctly left alone: TN ÷ (TN + FP).
specificity.more: Its denominator is the bottom row of the matrix. Lecture §4.

precision.short: Of the patients the model flagged, the share who actually had the outcome: TP ÷ (TP + FP).
precision.more: It shares TP with sensitivity but not the denominator: everyone flagged, not everyone with the outcome. It falls when the outcome is rarer. Lecture §4.

fpr.short: Of the patients who did not have the outcome, the share who got a false alarm: FP ÷ (FP + TN). FPR = 1 − specificity.
fpr.more: FPR is not “the share of flags that were wrong”; that is 1 − precision, with a different denominator. Lecture §4.

f1.short: The harmonic mean of precision and sensitivity: high only when both are high.
f1.more: What F1 leaves out: it ignores the true negatives, and it treats a missed case and a false alarm as equally costly. Lecture §5.

undefined.short: A metric whose denominator is 0, such as precision when no one is flagged (0 ÷ 0). Show it as “undefined”, never as 0.
undefined.more: m11 returns null (JavaScript) or None (Python) for these. Lecture §4 and §6.

flagged-per-100.short: How many patients out of every 100 the model flags at a threshold: (TP + FP) ÷ all × 100. It is the workload the flag creates.
flagged-per-100.more: Lecture §7 uses calls per 100 discharges to pick a threshold for a team's capacity.

threshold-for-the-job.short: A threshold chosen with the people who act on the flag: their capacity, what a missed case costs, or a target sensitivity.
threshold-for-the-job.more: The best cut-off depends on the job, not on accuracy. The most accurate thresholds often flag almost no one. Lecture §7.

diabetes-rule.short: Among development out-of-fold thresholds where sensitivity is at least 0.90, choose the one with the highest specificity.
diabetes-rule.more: If two thresholds tie on specificity, m11 chooses the one with the higher sensitivity. The rule is applied to development data only, never to the test set (lecture §15).

roc-curve.short: Every threshold at once: each one gives a (false positive rate, true positive rate) point, and the curve joins them.
roc-curve.more: A useful model bows toward the top-left. The diagonal is random ranking: it catches patients with and without the outcome at the same rate. Lecture §8.

auroc.short: The area under the ROC curve: the chance that a random patient with the outcome gets a higher probability than a random patient without it. It describes ranking.
auroc.more: 0.5 is random ranking. AUROC is not accuracy, it doesn't choose the threshold, and it doesn't change when you move the threshold. There is no universal good value: it depends on the job. Lecture §9–10.

calibration-plot.short: Patients sorted by predicted probability and cut into 10 equal-size groups. Each dot compares a group's mean prediction with the share who actually had the outcome.
calibration-plot.more: Dots near the diagonal mean the probabilities can be read as risks. Good ranking (high AUROC) does not guarantee this: halving every probability keeps AUROC but moves every dot off the diagonal. Lecture §10.

prevalence-baseline.short: A “model” that gives every patient the same probability: the share of positives in its training rows. AUROC 0.5.
prevalence-baseline.more: Lecture §16 draws it as the chance line. In scikit-learn: DummyClassifier(strategy="prior").

logistic-regression.short: A weighted sum of the features, squeezed into a probability between 0 and 1 by an S-shaped curve.
logistic-regression.more: A classifier despite its name. Simple and checkable; it misses curved or combined effects unless you add them. Lecture §11–12.

random-forest.short: Many decision trees, each grown on a different sample of patients; the probability is the average of the trees' probabilities.
random-forest.more: Lecture §11. Here: 300 trees, at least 3 training patients per leaf.

gradient-boosting.short: Trees added in sequence, each one fixing the errors the earlier trees left.
gradient-boosting.more: Lecture §11. Here: LightGBM with its default settings, as in the lecture.

knn.short: A patient's probability is the share of positives among the k most similar training patients. Here k = 25.
knn.more: “Similar” means close in distance across all features, so features must be on the same scale. Small k follows individual patients closely; large k smooths.

svm.short: Draws the boundary that separates the two classes with the widest possible gap. A patient's raw score is their signed distance from that boundary.
svm.more: The raw score is not a probability. Higher means “more likely positive”, but you can't read it as a chance; the supplied helper converts it. Lecture §1 warns about scores like this.

raw-score.short: A number a model outputs that ranks patients but is not a probability, such as an SVM's distance from its boundary.
raw-score.more: Higher still means “more likely”, but don't read it as a chance. Lecture §1.

pipeline.short: One object that holds every step that learns from data (encoding, filling in missing values, scaling) plus the model, so cross-validation refits all of them inside each training fold.

scaling.short: Putting every feature on the same scale (here: subtract the training mean, divide by the training standard deviation).
scaling.more: kNN and SVM use distances, so a feature measured in large units would otherwise dominate. The scaler must learn its means from training rows only, inside the pipeline.

imputation.short: Filling in missing values. Here each blank becomes the median of that feature in the training rows.
imputation.more: Learned from data, so it belongs inside the pipeline. Lecture §14.

training-auroc.short: AUROC on the patients a model learned from. It flatters every model.
training-auroc.more: A big gap between training and CV AUROC means the model memorised its training patients. Lecture §13.

development-set.short: The 80% of rows you train on and make every choice with: models, thresholds, everything.
development-set.more: Marked split = dev in each CSV, with a fold number 1–5.

test-set.short: The 20% of rows locked at the start and used once, at the end, to confirm the choices you already made.
test-set.more: Once you've looked at it and changed something, it is no longer unseen. Lecture §13.

cross-validation.short: Splitting the development rows into 5 folds and training 5 times: each time one fold is held out and scored by a model that never saw it.
cross-validation.more: Every development patient is validated exactly once. Cross-validation is for choosing; the test set is for confirming. Lecture §13.

fold.short: One of the 5 groups the development rows are split into. The fold column in each CSV is fixed: every model uses the same folds.
fold.more: Lecture §14, rule 1: same splits, same metrics.

oof.short: A development patient's probability from the cross-validation round in which their fold was held out, so the model never saw them.
oof.more: Your app's development results are all out-of-fold: label them “Development (OOF)”.

cv-auroc.short: AUROC on each held-out fold, summarised as the mean ± SD of the 5 folds.
cv-auroc.more: A cross-validated result, never a test result. Lecture §13 and §16.

fold-sd.short: The average of the 5 fold AUROCs, and their standard deviation: how much the score moves from one fold to another.
fold-sd.more: A small dataset gives a wide SD. Lecture §16.

within-one-sd.short: A model's lead over logistic regression is no bigger than logistic regression's fold-to-fold SD. A lead that small is within the noise: weak evidence that one model is better.
within-one-sd.more: Lecture §16: when results are close, prefer the simpler model. The order used here, simplest first: logreg, kNN, SVM, random forest, gradient boosting.

five-rules.term: Five rules for a fair comparison
five-rules.short: Same folds for every model; preprocessing inside a pipeline; no leaked columns; each patient's records kept together; test set locked until the end.
five-rules.more: Without them, the “winner” may just be the model that saw more of the answers. None of these mistakes raises an error. Lecture §14.

leaked-column.short: A column derived from, or recorded after, the outcome. It gives the model the answer, so the score looks far better than it will be on new patients.
leaked-column.more: Example: HbA1c defines the diabetes label. Check every column's “When is it known?” entry against the prediction point. Lecture §14.

when-known.short: The data dictionary's entry saying when each value exists, relative to the moment the prediction is made.
when-known.more: A predictor must be known at the prediction point. Anything known only at or after the outcome is a leak.

records-together.short: If a patient has several records, all of them go in the same fold. Otherwise the model is tested on people it has already seen.
records-together.more: Each dataset here has one row per person, so this rule is met by design. Lecture §14.

peeking.short: Setting a threshold, a model or any other choice while looking at the test patients. It promises a result you won't get on new patients.
peeking.more: Set the threshold on development data only. Lecture §15.

clinical-lead.short: Your app's reader: someone who knows the clinical problem but not the metrics, and who must decide whether to use a model.
clinical-lead.more: Write for them: plain words, every metric's denominator said in patients, and every number labelled with where it comes from.

decisions-md.short: The file where you save each decision before you see the results it depends on, in four fixed sections.
decisions-md.more: The workflow reads it, and refuses to train or test until the right section is filled in and committed.

results-files.short: The JSON files in results/ that the Python workflow writes. Your app reads only these.
results-files.more: Commit and push results/ so your hosted app can load them.

public-link.short: A web address anyone can open without signing in, such as https://you.github.io/judge-the-model/.
public-link.more: Test it in a private or incognito window.

github-backup.short: Your code, data, results and DECISIONS.md, pushed to GitHub. It is your backup and what you submit.
github-backup.more: A commit on your laptop isn't a backup until it's pushed. The git history also shows that you saved your decisions before each stage.

static-site.short: A website made only of files (HTML, CSS, JavaScript and data). GitHub Pages hosts these; it can't run Python.
static-site.more: That's why the analysis runs on your computer and the app reads the exported results.
